transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. Um, honestly, I’m here because my sleep has just... it’s basically completely fallen apart. And I mean, it’s not just a bad night here or there, it’s every night. I’ll just lie there in bed in my apartment for hours. Literally hours. Like, I’ll have my laptop closed, I put it away on the nightstand, I try to do all the things you’re supposed to do to wind down, right? But my brain just absolutely won't stop. 

I'm just lying there in the dark, still mentally rechecking all my work deadlines—because my job has a million moving parts and if I drop one thing, the whole project stalls—and then my mind just immediately jumps from that to my tuition payments, and then to my class assignments, and I’m just running through these lists over and over and over again in my head. I try to force myself to stop thinking about it, but I can't. And the worst part is, even when I finally do manage to drift off, which takes forever, I wake up the next morning feeling like I never really turned off. Like my brain was just humming in the background the entire night, still working on those same problems. I just feel so completely drained before I even get out of bed, and I really don't know how to make it stop.
Is it only work and school-related things that you worry about at night, or do you also worry about other everyday things?

Oh, no, it's... it's definitely not just work and school, although those are the big ones that usually start the whole cycle. But once my brain gets going, it's like... it's like a snowball rolling downhill, you know? It just picks up everything else along the way. 

So, yeah, it starts with work—like, am I falling behind on that big quarterly analysis? Did I miss a data point that's going to make the whole report wrong? But then it immediately shifts to school, and I'll start agonizing over whether I'm just completely wasting my money on this degree. Like, is it even going to help me advance, or am I just burying myself in debt for no reason? And then, because I'm thinking about failing at work and wasting money on school, my mind just naturally jumps to my family. I start obsessing over what they're going to think of me. I'll just lie there convinced that they're all secretly talking about how I can't handle things, how I'm in over my head, how I'm 29 and I should have everything figured out by now but I clearly don't. 

And it's exhausting because it doesn't even have to be a big thing. It can be the smallest, most insignificant issue, like... I don't know, forgetting to reply to an email from a coworker or realizing I need to get my car's oil changed. Normal people just handle that stuff, right? But for me, in the middle of the night, I treat every single small issue like it's this massive, catastrophic event that's going to completely derail my entire future. It all feels so heavy and so urgent, and I just can't shut off the feeling that everything is on the verge of collapsing.
Do you ever experience sudden, intense episodes of fear or discomfort that reach a peak within minutes?

Sudden? Um... no, not really sudden. Like, I think I know what you mean, like when people suddenly feel like the world is ending right that second and it comes out of nowhere? I don't really get that. For me, it's not this out-of-the-blue spike that just hits me and peaks in a few minutes and then goes away. It's more like... well, it's just always there. It's this constant, heavy dread that just sits with me from the moment my alarm goes off until the moment I finally manage to pass out at night. 

It doesn't really peak, if that makes sense, because it never really drops. It just kind of simmers all day long. Like, I'll be at my desk, running my management analyses, looking at all the variables for a project, and the worry is just humming right there in the background the whole time. It's a slow burn. It's not a sudden rush of terror at all. It's just... relentless. So, no, I wouldn't say I have those sudden episodes where it peaks really fast. It's just a continuous loop that never really gives me a break. I'm already always operating at this ridiculously high baseline of stress, you know? So I don't really get the sudden waves, just... the constant ocean of it, I guess.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or activities because of your worries?

Um... avoiding things? No, actually, I don't think I do that. I mean, don't get me wrong, I *want* to. There are definitely mornings—like, honestly, pretty much every single morning at this point—where the thought of getting up and facing my inbox, or dealing with the project managers, or looking at my coursework just feels completely impossible. I'll lie there thinking how easy it would be to just call in sick and hide from the world. But I never actually do it. I never avoid it. 

If anything, it’s almost the exact opposite. Because I’m so terrified of dropping the ball or missing a deadline, I force myself to be hyper-involved in everything. Like, if there’s a big data review for one of my management analyses at work, I won’t skip the meeting or try to get someone else to cover it. I’ll be sitting right there at the table, completely dreading it, running through every single possible scenario of how I might have messed up the variables or misinterpreted a trend, just agonizing over it the entire time I'm sitting there. 

And it’s the exact same way with my degree. I don’t skip lectures or put off my assignments, even though just thinking about the classes and whether I'm wasting my tuition money makes me feel incredibly stressed. I just sit at my laptop and force myself to do the work while my brain is just constantly humming with all those worries I told you about. I feel like if I actually started avoiding things, that would just give me a whole new list of things to worry about, right? Like, then I’d be obsessing over the consequences of missing work, or dodging my family's calls and what they think about me avoiding them. So I just show up to everything. I go to the office, I do the schoolwork, I answer every single email... I just do it all while carrying around this massive, exhausting weight of dread. So, no, I don't avoid the situations... I just kind of suffer through them.
Have you experienced any significant changes in your mood or interest in activities you normally enjoy?

Um... mood changes? Or losing interest in things? I don't... I don't really think so. I mean, it's kind of hard to tell sometimes, just because I'm so exhausted all the time from the worrying, you know? But I wouldn't say I've lost interest in the things I actually like doing. It's just that I don't really have the time or the mental energy for them right now. 

Like, I used to love going to this little pottery studio downtown on the weekends. It was just a fun, creative outlet, nothing serious. And I haven't gone in months, but it's not because I don't *want* to go, or because I don't care about it anymore. It's just that when Saturday rolls around, my brain is already running through all the management analyses I have to finish by Monday, and I'm obsessing over my school assignments, and I just feel like I can't justify taking three hours to go play with clay when I have all this other stuff hanging over my head. I'd just be sitting at the pottery wheel stressing about my quarterly reports anyway. 

So the interest is definitely still there. I still want to do those things. I still care about them. And as for my mood... I mean, I wouldn't say I'm depressed or anything like that. I don't feel hopeless or sad or empty. I just feel... wired. And tired. Like, constantly on edge. But my actual mood, when I'm not actively spiraling about work or school or what my family thinks of me—which, granted, isn't very often these days—but when I do get a moment, I feel like my normal self. I still laugh at the same jokes, I still enjoy talking to my friends when I actually have the energy to text them back. It's just that the anxiety is so loud and takes up so much space that everything else kind of gets pushed to the margins. But no, I wouldn't say my actual mood has changed, or that I've lost interest in my hobbies. I'm just... I'm just too overwhelmed to engage with them right now, if that makes sense.
Do you experience any physical symptoms like tremors, sweating, or rapid heartbeat when you're worrying?

Tremors? Like, shaking? Um... no. No, I don't really get anything like that. Sweating or the rapid heartbeat... honestly, no. It's actually kind of weird, because you'd think with how much my brain is just absolutely spinning all the time, my body would be reacting to it, right? Like, you'd think my heart would be pounding out of my chest when I'm sitting there agonizing over whether I completely ruined the quarterly projections for the project managers. But it really doesn't. 

I'll just be sitting there at my desk, staring at my dual monitors, and on the outside, I probably look completely fine. My hands don't shake when I'm typing—I mean, thank goodness, because I have to do so much data entry and typing for my coursework, too, so if my hands were trembling all day, that would just be a logistical nightmare on top of everything else. And I don't get all sweaty or flushed either. My heart rate feels... well, normal, I guess. I've never really felt it racing or fluttering or doing anything out of the ordinary. 

It's almost entirely just... in my head. It's like my brain is running a marathon at full speed, constantly tripping over all these worst-case scenarios about work and school, but my actual physical body is just sitting there in the office chair, completely still. Sometimes I think it would almost make more sense if I did have those physical things happen, because then at least there would be some sort of visible proof of how intensely I'm worrying, you know? Like people could look at me and say, 'Oh, she's sweating, her heart is racing, she must be really stressed out.' But because I don't have the tremors or the pounding chest, nobody really knows what's going on with me. I just look like a totally normal analyst quietly doing her job. So, yeah, no... I don't really notice any of those physical things you mentioned at all.
Do you have recurring, intrusive thoughts that you feel compelled to repeat or ritualize in your daily life?

Rituals? Like... having to do a specific action over and over again? Um, no. I mean, my thoughts are definitely recurring, like I was saying earlier, because I'm literally always thinking about work or my coursework or whether I'm doing enough. But I don't feel forced to actually *do* anything about them, like a routine. 

Like, I don't have to go check the locks on my door five times before I leave for the office, and I don't have to repeat a specific phrase out loud to make the bad thoughts go away. It's nothing like that. It's more just... a constant stream of worrying that I can't turn off. I'll be sitting there staring at my spreadsheets for my management analyses, and my brain will just be looping through all the ways I could get fired or fail my classes, but I don't have any routines I have to perform to fix it. I just sit there and worry.

Actually, it's funny you ask that, because my roommate in undergrad used to have to organize her desk a very specific way before she could study, like her pens and notebooks had to be perfectly parallel, and if someone bumped the table, she had to start all over again. But I'm not like that at all. My desk at work is actually kind of a mess right now with all the printouts and sticky notes, which probably doesn't help my stress levels, to be honest, but I don't have any rules about how it has to look or anything I have to touch a certain number of times. 

So yeah, the thoughts just kind of live in my head. They're definitely intrusive, because I certainly don't *want* to be thinking about them, and they constantly interrupt whatever I'm trying to focus on. But they don't come with any sort of ritual. I just sort of... let them play on a loop while I try to get through my day.
Do you often feel restless or on edge when you're worrying?

Restless? Or on edge? Um... well... I guess I'm not really sure what you mean by that, to be honest. Like, I don't feel like I have to jump up and pace around the room or anything. I'm not fidgeting constantly or feeling like I can't sit still. I mean, I sit at my desk for like ten hours a day, just staring at my monitors, so I'm definitely capable of being still. 

And "on edge"... I don't know. I feel stressed, obviously, and exhausted, like I mentioned before. But I wouldn't say I feel like I'm waiting for something to jump out at me, or like I'm startled easily, if that's what you mean. I'm just so bogged down by all the things I have to do and all the ways I could mess them up. It's more of a heavy feeling than a jumpy feeling. 

Like, yesterday, I was trying to finish up this massive dataset for one of the project managers, and I was just sitting there, totally frozen, just spiraling about whether I had formatted the pivot tables wrong and if it was going to throw off the whole quarterly projection. And I just sat there. I didn't feel restless, I just felt... stuck. Just completely paralyzed by the worry. So, no, I don't think I really feel restless or on edge. I just feel overwhelmed.
Has your worrying been interfering with your relationships or daily activities in any way?

Yeah, it definitely is. It's actually getting pretty bad, if I'm being completely honest. I mean, at work, I've actually started missing deadlines, which is just... it's so unlike me. I used to be the person who had everything submitted to the project managers two days early. But now, because I'm just sitting there second-guessing every single cell in my spreadsheets and getting paralyzed by all the what-ifs, I'm turning things in late. Like last week, I was supposed to have this variance report done by Thursday at noon, and I just couldn't hit the button to send it because I was so worried the formatting was wrong, and I ended up sending it Friday afternoon. My manager definitely noticed, and of course, that just gave me something new to worry about all weekend. 

And it's bleeding into my coursework, too. I'm taking these certificate classes—just to try and stay competitive, you know, since everyone has a bachelor's these days and you really need specialized certs to move up—and I am just falling so far behind. I have lectures I haven't even watched from three weeks ago. Every time I open the student portal, my brain just starts screaming about how I'm going to fail the modules anyway, or how I'm too far behind to ever catch up, so I just close the tab. 

And as for my daily life outside of that... I mean, my whole personal routine is just entirely gone. I used to be so good about doing things that kept me grounded. Like, I would go running almost every morning. I had this great three-mile loop around my neighborhood, right past the park, and it was just a nice, quiet way to start the day before looking at screens. I haven't done that in months. My running shoes are just gathering dust by the door. And I used to do yoga, too, like actual studio classes twice a week to just stretch out my back from sitting at my desk all day. But now, by the time work is over, I'm just so mentally exhausted from the constant worrying that I can't even fathom going to a class. I just go straight to the couch. 

Oh, and cooking... that's completely out the window. I used to meal prep every single Sunday. I'd make these big batches of quinoa and roasted vegetables and portion them out for the week so I'd have healthy lunches at the office. I actually used to really enjoy the process of chopping everything and following a recipe. Now? I'm literally just ordering takeout or eating dry cereal for dinner because the thought of planning a meal, going to the grocery store, and actually standing in the kitchen cooking it just feels like climbing Mount Everest. It's just... I don't know, it's like the worry takes up so much space in my head and drains so much of my energy that there's no room left for anything else, not even the stuff that used to make me feel like a normal, functioning person. So, yeah, it's definitely interfering. A lot.
Are you feeling like your worrying is significantly affecting your ability to function in your daily life or causing a lot of distress for you?

Yeah, I mean, exactly like I was just saying... it really is. It’s completely tanking my ability to function normally, and it is incredibly distressing. 

Like I mentioned with missing those work deadlines... that causes me so much distress on its own, just watching it happen. I'm sitting there at my desk, knowing I'm falling behind, knowing my manager is probably wondering what on earth is wrong with me lately because I used to be the reliable one. I used to be the analyst everyone came to when they needed something done fast and done right. And with those certificate classes, I mean, I paid good money for those modules, and I'm just watching myself fail because I can't even function well enough to open the student portal without spiraling into a panic about my future. 

So, yes, the distress is... it's massive. It's almost like a secondary layer of worry, you know? I worry about the actual tasks, and then I worry about how much the worrying is ruining my life. Because I look at the fact that I've stopped doing all those routines that used to keep me grounded—like I said, I've completely abandoned my yoga classes, I haven't gone on a run in months, I can't even bring myself to cook a basic meal or meal-prep like I used to—and it just makes me feel pathetic, honestly. 

It's like I'm watching myself forget how to be a functioning adult. I used to have it all together, with the morning runs, the healthy lunches in the fridge, the early project submissions. And now I can barely function enough to get off the couch and pour a bowl of cereal for dinner. So, yeah, "significantly affecting my ability to function" is probably the most accurate way to put it. It's just so upsetting to feel like you're losing control over your own life and your own routines, and I just... I really don't know how to get back to the person who could actually do all those things without feeling so paralyzed all the time.
Has your worrying affected your relationships with friends or family in any way?

Um... friends or family? I mean... no, not really? Or at least, not in the way you might think. Like, we aren't getting into arguments or anything like that. I'm not snapping at people or having these big dramatic fallouts. 

With my parents, they live a couple states over, so our relationship is mostly just our regular Sunday afternoon phone calls. And I still do those, I still pick up the phone every week. I just... I guess I just put on a really good brave face for them. I don't want them to know how much I'm spiraling about work or how far behind I am on those certificate classes, because they were just so incredibly proud of me when I landed this management analyst role right out of school. They brag about it to their neighbors and everything. So I just smile through the phone and tell them work is busy but great, and they tell me about their garden or whatever, and that's that. So that relationship is totally fine, it's just maybe a bit surface-level right now because I feel like I have to hide all of this overwhelming worry from them.

And then with my friends... honestly, I'm just not really seeing them. But again, it's not because we're fighting. It's just that, exactly like I was saying about being so exhausted and going straight to the couch... I just do not have it in me to socialize. My friend Sarah keeps inviting me to this Thursday trivia night at a brewery downtown that we used to go to all the time, and I just keep making up excuses every single week. I tell her I have to study for my modules—which is almost funny in a sad way, since I'm not actually studying, I'm just avoiding the portal—or I tell her I have to work late on a variance report. And she is so incredibly sweet about it, she always just tells me not to worry and that we will catch up next time. She isn't mad at me at all. 

So, yeah, no real issues or drama with anyone in my life. I guess I'm just sort of... absent. I'm not actively damaging my relationships, I just literally do not have the mental energy or the space in my brain to actually participate in them right now.
Do you feel like your worrying is impacting your ability to maintain relationships or perform at work?

Well, exactly, yeah. I feel like I’m kind of repeating myself a bit, but yes, it absolutely is impacting my ability to perform at work, and to maintain my relationships, just... all of it. 

Like I was saying about work, I’ve started missing those deadlines, which, for someone in my position as a management analyst, is basically the worst thing you can do. My whole job relies on me being sharp and on time, and I'm just not right now. And falling so far behind in my certificate classes... that just adds this whole other layer of guilt on top of everything. I sit there and think about how much money I spent on those classes and how I'm just throwing it away because I can't get my brain to stop spinning long enough to watch a lecture. 

And then, because I'm so drained from all of that panic at work and with school, I have absolutely nothing left in the tank for my friends or my family. I'm just a ghost. I can't maintain those connections when I can't even maintain my own basic life, you know? I mean, like I was telling you, I've completely stopped doing all those routines that used to keep me grounded. The yoga studio I used to go to probably thinks I moved away, and my running shoes haven't moved from the hallway in months. Even cooking, which used to be my Sunday ritual... I just can't do it. I can't do any of it. So yes, my performance at work is slipping, my classes are a disaster, and my relationships are basically on pause because I just don't have the capacity to keep any of those plates spinning right now.
Are there any areas in your life where you feel like your worrying is holding you back from achieving your goals or fulfilling your responsibilities?

I know I probably sound like a broken record at this point, because I feel like I just keep circling back to the exact same examples, but... yes. Absolutely. It is holding me back in basically every single area of my life. 

When you ask about responsibilities, the very first thing my mind goes to is work. Being a management analyst, my entire role is built on being reliable and delivering data on time, so missing those work deadlines like I’ve started doing recently... that is me completely failing my core responsibilities. I sit at my desk and I know I should be doing the work, but I just can't get past the panic, and it’s terrifying to watch yourself fail at something you used to be so good at. 

And then with my goals... well, that’s exactly what those certificate classes were supposed to be. I didn't just sign up for them on a whim. I have my bachelor's, but I really wanted to push myself, you know? I wanted to get those extra credentials to maybe move up to a senior role eventually, or at least just broaden my skill set. That was a huge, concrete goal I set for myself this year. But because I'm falling so far behind in the classes, I'm basically just watching that goal slip right through my fingers while I waste the tuition money. 

And honestly, it's not even just the professional or educational stuff. It’s my personal goals, too. My responsibility to just... take care of myself. Like I was saying before, I’ve completely stopped doing all the routines that used to keep me grounded. I haven't been to yoga, I haven't gone for a run, I don't even cook anymore... and cooking used to be this whole Sunday ritual for me to prep for the week and make sure I was eating healthy. Now I just can't bring myself to do any of it. So when you ask if it's holding me back, it's just... it's holding me back from everything. My career, my education, my health... all of it is just completely stalled out because I can't get out of my own head.
Do you feel like your worrying is making it difficult for you to enjoy or participate in activities that you normally find pleasurable?

I know I keep bringing up the exact same things, and I'm so sorry, I probably sound completely broken at this point, but... yes. It really is. The things I used to actually enjoy? They're just gone from my life right now. 

Like I mentioned before with my running shoes and the yoga studio... I used to genuinely love those things. Yoga wasn't just a workout for me, it was something I looked forward to all week. I had this specific Tuesday night class, and it was just this perfect, quiet hour where I didn't have to think. And cooking! Cooking was my absolute favorite thing to do. I used to go get fresh ingredients on Sunday mornings and spend hours in the kitchen just chopping vegetables and listening to podcasts or music. It was so pleasurable, it was my happy place, you know? It was how I grounded myself for the week ahead. 

But now... I can't even fathom doing any of that. Because if I try to roll out my yoga mat, or if I even look at a recipe, my brain immediately starts screaming at me about everything else. It's like, "How can you stand here chopping onions when you are missing major work deadlines?" Or, "How can you justify going for a run when you are falling so incredibly far behind in your certificate classes?" 

The guilt just completely consumes me. Because I know I’m missing those crucial deadlines at work, and I know I'm basically failing those classes I paid so much for, any time I try to do something just for fun or to relax, the worry completely hijacks it. It's like my brain is telling me I don't deserve to enjoy things or take a break because I'm failing at my responsibilities. So I've just stopped doing all those grounding routines completely. I don't run, I don't cook, I don't go to yoga. I just sit on the couch worrying about work and school. It's miserable, honestly. The worry has just put up this giant wall between me and anything that used to bring me joy, because all my mental space is just tied up in how badly I'm dropping the ball everywhere else.
Are you feeling like your worrying is causing you significant distress or interfering with your daily life in a major way?

I know, I know, I keep bringing up the exact same examples, and I really am sorry for just repeating myself over and over today, but I just want to make sure you understand how total this is. It’s not just a little distress, it’s... it’s completely paralyzing. So, yes, it is interfering with my life in the most major way possible, because my life basically doesn't even look like my life anymore. 

When you ask about significant distress, I can't even fully describe the pit in my stomach when I look at my computer screen every morning. Being a management analyst means people are literally waiting on my reports to make their own decisions, and the fact that I’ve started missing those work deadlines... it physically makes me sick to my stomach. I sit at my desk, and I'm just paralyzed by it. And then I think about falling so horribly behind in my certificate classes, and the distress just compounds. It’s this intense, agonizing guilt that wakes me up in the middle of the night. I just lie there in the dark thinking about the tuition money I've wasted and how I'm actively sabotaging my own future because I can't get it together to just watch a recorded lecture. 

And as for interfering with my daily life... my entire daily life used to be built on those routines I was telling you about. They were the scaffolding that held my week together. Cooking on Sundays wasn't just about making food, it was how I ensured I was eating properly and taking care of myself. Yoga and running were how I burned off the tension. And now that I've stopped doing all of those things that used to keep me grounded, I have absolutely no structure left. I don't chop vegetables, I don't lace up my sneakers, I don't roll out my mat. I literally just exist in this constant, exhausting state of pure panic. I don't do anything but worry about the deadlines I'm blowing and the classes I'm failing. So, yeah, the interference is... it's total. It has completely taken over every single hour of my day.
Are there any areas of your life where you feel like your worrying is significantly impairing your ability to function or perform?

I feel like I’m losing my mind a little bit because I know I keep giving you the exact same examples, and I'm really sorry to just keep repeating myself, but... yes. Yes, it's impairing my ability to function in literally every way a person *can* function. 

When you use the word "perform," that really hits a nerve for me, because performance is basically my entire identity right now. I'm a management analyst. My whole job is to analyze data, write reports, and deliver them to management so they can make decisions. That is my function. But lately, I'll open up a dashboard or a spreadsheet, and the worry just floods my system so fast and so intensely that I can't even process the numbers on the screen. I just sit there, completely paralyzed, watching the clock tick down. So, like I've been saying, I’ve started missing these crucial work deadlines. I am literally failing to perform the basic duties of my job. 

And then I log off, and I try to function as a student, and I just... I can't do that either. I'm falling so horribly behind in my certificate classes because I can't even get myself to perform the simple task of logging into the portal and hitting "play" on a recorded lecture. I just sit there staring at the login screen, completely overwhelmed by how far behind I am and how much money I'm wasting. 

And it's not even just the professional or academic performance, you know? It's my basic ability to function as a healthy human being. I can't even maintain my own life anymore. I’ve completely stopped doing all the routines that used to keep me grounded. I used to be someone who functioned so well—I was organized, I went to my Tuesday yoga class, I went running, I did my big Sunday meal prep and cooking to make sure I had healthy lunches for the week. I was on top of things. But now? I can't even manage to chop a single vegetable or put on my running shoes. The worry just drains every single ounce of my ability to actually *do* anything. It takes up so much space in my brain that there's nothing left over to actually run my life. So, yes, the impairment is... it's total. I'm just not functioning at all.
Are there any situations or activities that you avoid because of your worrying?

Avoid? Um... I don't... I'm not really sure if "avoid" is the right word for it, to be honest. Like, I don't think I'm actively avoiding anything, if that makes sense? 

Because when you say avoid, I guess I picture someone who is, I don't know, terrified of elevators so they take the stairs, or someone who is actively hiding from a specific person or a specific place. And it's really not like that for me at all. I'm not scared of my kitchen, or the yoga studio, or the running trail at the park. I don't look at my running shoes and feel afraid of them. I'm not dodging specific places or social situations because they make me worry... because the worry is just already there, 24/7, no matter where I am. It's just living inside my head. 

So, no, I haven't really noticed any specific situations I'm avoiding. It really all just goes back to what I was just saying about being completely paralyzed. I'm not avoiding the grocery store on Sunday mornings, I just... I literally can't get myself off the couch to go, because I'm so consumed by the guilt of the management reports I haven't finished and the certificate lectures I haven't watched. If I could just snap my fingers and make the guilt stop, I would be out the door in a heartbeat. I'd love to go back to my Tuesday night class. I'm definitely not avoiding it. I'm just... I'm just trapped under the weight of everything I'm dropping the ball on, so I just stay home and stare at the wall. But I wouldn't call it avoidance, I don't think. I just don't have the bandwidth to do anything else.
Are there any activities or situations that you used to enjoy or participate in, but now find yourself avoiding because of your worrying?

I feel like maybe I'm not explaining myself right, because we're kind of circling back to that word again, but... I really, truly don't think I'm avoiding the things I used to enjoy. 

And I *did* enjoy them, so much. Like I was saying before, my Tuesday yoga class, my Sunday meal prep, going for runs... I loved all of that. It was my time. It was how I kept myself sane. But I'm not avoiding them because of the worry. Like, the worry isn't *about* the yoga or the cooking, and I'm definitely not actively trying to stay away from them. 

It's more like... okay, imagine you have this massive, crushing weight sitting right on your chest. You aren't *avoiding* standing up, you literally just can't get up. That's what the worry about my job and my classes does to me right now. I'll be sitting there on the couch, and I'll think, "I should go for a run. I used to love running. It would probably clear my head." But then I immediately think about the dashboard I didn't update for the management team, or the recorded lecture I'm three weeks behind on for my certificate, and my chest just tightens up, and I can't move. I just sit there. I want to do those things. I really, really do. I miss my life. I miss feeling like a normal person who chops vegetables and goes outside. But I'm not dodging those activities or avoiding them, I'm just completely immobilized by the guilt of everything else I'm failing at. So, no, I wouldn't say I avoid them at all. I just can't get to them.

target_item.manifestation: I’ve started missing work deadlines and falling behind in my certificate classes, and I’ve stopped doing the routines that used to keep me grounded, like yoga, running, and cooking.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty participating in normally pleasurable activities, which directly relates to my functional impairment where I've stopped doing routines that used to keep me grounded, like yoga, running, and cooking.

patient.answer:
I know I keep bringing up the exact same things, and I'm so sorry, I probably sound completely broken at this point, but... yes. It really is. The things I used to actually enjoy? They're just gone from my life right now. 

Like I mentioned before with my running shoes and the yoga studio... I used to genuinely love those things. Yoga wasn't just a workout for me, it was something I looked forward to all week. I had this specific Tuesday night class, and it was just this perfect, quiet hour where I didn't have to think. And cooking! Cooking was my absolute favorite thing to do. I used to go get fresh ingredients on Sunday mornings and spend hours in the kitchen just chopping vegetables and listening to podcasts or music. It was so pleasurable, it was my happy place, you know? It was how I grounded myself for the week ahead. 

But now... I can't even fathom doing any of that. Because if I try to roll out my yoga mat, or if I even look at a recipe, my brain immediately starts screaming at me about everything else. It's like, "How can you stand here chopping onions when you are missing major work deadlines?" Or, "How can you justify going for a run when you are falling so incredibly far behind in your certificate classes?" 

The guilt just completely consumes me. Because I know I’m missing those crucial deadlines at work, and I know I'm basically failing those classes I paid so much for, any time I try to do something just for fun or to relax, the worry completely hijacks it. It's like my brain is telling me I don't deserve to enjoy things or take a break because I'm failing at my responsibilities. So I've just stopped doing all those grounding routines completely. I don't run, I don't cook, I don't go to yoga. I just sit on the couch worrying about work and school. It's miserable, honestly. The worry has just put up this giant wall between me and anything that used to bring me joy, because all my mental space is just tied up in how badly I'm dropping the ball everywhere else.

doctor.question: Are you feeling like your worrying is causing you significant distress or interfering with your daily life in a major way?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve started missing work deadlines and falling behind in my certificate classes, and I’ve stopped doing the routines that used to keep me grounded, like yoga, running, and cooking.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the worrying is causing significant distress or interfering with daily life, which maps directly to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I know, I know, I keep bringing up the exact same examples, and I really am sorry for just repeating myself over and over today, but I just want to make sure you understand how total this is. It’s not just a little distress, it’s... it’s completely paralyzing. So, yes, it is interfering with my life in the most major way possible, because my life basically doesn't even look like my life anymore. 

When you ask about significant distress, I can't even fully describe the pit in my stomach when I look at my computer screen every morning. Being a management analyst means people are literally waiting on my reports to make their own decisions, and the fact that I’ve started missing those work deadlines... it physically makes me sick to my stomach. I sit at my desk, and I'm just paralyzed by it. And then I think about falling so horribly behind in my certificate classes, and the distress just compounds. It’s this intense, agonizing guilt that wakes me up in the middle of the night. I just lie there in the dark thinking about the tuition money I've wasted and how I'm actively sabotaging my own future because I can't get it together to just watch a recorded lecture. 

And as for interfering with my daily life... my entire daily life used to be built on those routines I was telling you about. They were the scaffolding that held my week together. Cooking on Sundays wasn't just about making food, it was how I ensured I was eating properly and taking care of myself. Yoga and running were how I burned off the tension. And now that I've stopped doing all of those things that used to keep me grounded, I have absolutely no structure left. I don't chop vegetables, I don't lace up my sneakers, I don't roll out my mat. I literally just exist in this constant, exhausting state of pure panic. I don't do anything but worry about the deadlines I'm blowing and the classes I'm failing. So, yeah, the interference is... it's total. It has completely taken over every single hour of my day.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing them significant impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life
doctor.question: Are there any areas of your life where you feel like your worrying is significantly impairing your ability to function or perform?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve started missing work deadlines and falling behind in my certificate classes, and I’ve stopped doing the routines that used to keep me grounded, like yoga, running, and cooking.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the worrying is significantly impairing my ability to function or perform, which directly assesses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I feel like I’m losing my mind a little bit because I know I keep giving you the exact same examples, and I'm really sorry to just keep repeating myself, but... yes. Yes, it's impairing my ability to function in literally every way a person *can* function. 

When you use the word "perform," that really hits a nerve for me, because performance is basically my entire identity right now. I'm a management analyst. My whole job is to analyze data, write reports, and deliver them to management so they can make decisions. That is my function. But lately, I'll open up a dashboard or a spreadsheet, and the worry just floods my system so fast and so intensely that I can't even process the numbers on the screen. I just sit there, completely paralyzed, watching the clock tick down. So, like I've been saying, I’ve started missing these crucial work deadlines. I am literally failing to perform the basic duties of my job. 

And then I log off, and I try to function as a student, and I just... I can't do that either. I'm falling so horribly behind in my certificate classes because I can't even get myself to perform the simple task of logging into the portal and hitting "play" on a recorded lecture. I just sit there staring at the login screen, completely overwhelmed by how far behind I am and how much money I'm wasting. 

And it's not even just the professional or academic performance, you know? It's my basic ability to function as a healthy human being. I can't even maintain my own life anymore. I’ve completely stopped doing all the routines that used to keep me grounded. I used to be someone who functioned so well—I was organized, I went to my Tuesday yoga class, I went running, I did my big Sunday meal prep and cooking to make sure I had healthy lunches for the week. I was on top of things. But now? I can't even manage to chop a single vegetable or put on my running shoes. The worry just drains every single ounce of my ability to actually *do* anything. It takes up so much space in my brain that there's nothing left over to actually run my life. So, yes, the impairment is... it's total. I'm just not functioning at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing significant avoidance behaviors
doctor.question: Are there any situations or activities that you avoid because of your worrying?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoidance behaviors related to worrying, which is not specifically covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Avoid? Um... I don't... I'm not really sure if "avoid" is the right word for it, to be honest. Like, I don't think I'm actively avoiding anything, if that makes sense? 

Because when you say avoid, I guess I picture someone who is, I don't know, terrified of elevators so they take the stairs, or someone who is actively hiding from a specific person or a specific place. And it's really not like that for me at all. I'm not scared of my kitchen, or the yoga studio, or the running trail at the park. I don't look at my running shoes and feel afraid of them. I'm not dodging specific places or social situations because they make me worry... because the worry is just already there, 24/7, no matter where I am. It's just living inside my head. 

So, no, I haven't really noticed any specific situations I'm avoiding. It really all just goes back to what I was just saying about being completely paralyzed. I'm not avoiding the grocery store on Sunday mornings, I just... I literally can't get myself off the couch to go, because I'm so consumed by the guilt of the management reports I haven't finished and the certificate lectures I haven't watched. If I could just snap my fingers and make the guilt stop, I would be out the door in a heartbeat. I'd love to go back to my Tuesday night class. I'm definitely not avoiding it. I'm just... I'm just trapped under the weight of everything I'm dropping the ball on, so I just stay home and stare at the wall. But I wouldn't call it avoidance, I don't think. I just don't have the bandwidth to do anything else.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's worrying is causing significant avoidance behaviors
doctor.question: Are there any activities or situations that you used to enjoy or participate in, but now find yourself avoiding because of your worrying?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoidance of activities or situations due to worrying, which is not a specific symptom listed in the patient's profile.

patient.answer:
I feel like maybe I'm not explaining myself right, because we're kind of circling back to that word again, but... I really, truly don't think I'm avoiding the things I used to enjoy. 

And I *did* enjoy them, so much. Like I was saying before, my Tuesday yoga class, my Sunday meal prep, going for runs... I loved all of that. It was my time. It was how I kept myself sane. But I'm not avoiding them because of the worry. Like, the worry isn't *about* the yoga or the cooking, and I'm definitely not actively trying to stay away from them. 

It's more like... okay, imagine you have this massive, crushing weight sitting right on your chest. You aren't *avoiding* standing up, you literally just can't get up. That's what the worry about my job and my classes does to me right now. I'll be sitting there on the couch, and I'll think, "I should go for a run. I used to love running. It would probably clear my head." But then I immediately think about the dashboard I didn't update for the management team, or the recorded lecture I'm three weeks behind on for my certificate, and my chest just tightens up, and I can't move. I just sit there. I want to do those things. I really, really do. I miss my life. I miss feeling like a normal person who chops vegetables and goes outside. But I'm not dodging those activities or avoiding them, I'm just completely immobilized by the guilt of everything else I'm failing at. So, no, I wouldn't say I avoid them at all. I just can't get to them.

My responsibilities are my job and my education, and my goals were to maintain a healthy, balanced lifestyle while advancing my career, and right now, all of that is just completely falling apart. Like I was saying a few minutes ago, I’ve started missing my work deadlines. I am a management analyst, so my entire job is to provide data so other people can do *their* jobs, and I am failing at that responsibility because I just sit at my desk frozen. 

And as for my goals? My main goal this year was to finish these certificate classes so I could maybe move up in my department, or at least just feel more confident in my data modeling, but instead, I’m falling horribly behind. I can't even get myself to watch a single recorded lecture. It's just a constant loop of worrying about how far behind I am, which makes me fall even further behind.

I’ve completely stopped doing all the daily and weekly routines that used to keep me grounded and healthy. I haven't been to my yoga class in I don't even know how long, I haven't gone running, I haven't done my Sunday meal prep or any actual cooking... and cooking used to be the way I set myself up for success for the whole week! It was how I made sure I was taking care of my body. Now I just can't bring myself to chop a single vegetable.
